headline: Turkish Fishermen and Conservationists Restore 300 Miles of Mediterranean Coast
meta_description: Local conservationists and fishermen in Türkiye tripled protected seascapes along 310 miles of coastline, bringing back sharks, seals, and healthy fish populat…
summary_short: With $3 million in funding, Turkish conservationists and fishermen expanded marine protection zones, reducing illegal fishing by 80% and restoring Mediterranean wildlife.
body:
When conservationist Zafer Kızılkaya and his team set out to protect Türkiye's Mediterranean coast between Gökova Bay and Cape Gelidonya in 2019, they faced a paradox: designated marine sanctuaries existed on paper, but without local enforcement and engagement, illegal fishing had decimated shark, seal, and turtle populations. The fishing communities who depended on these waters suffered alongside the wildlife—their catches dwindled as the ecosystem collapsed. The Endangered Landscapes & Seascapes Program, a nonprofit backed by the UK's billion-pound Arcadia Fund, awarded Kızılkaya's team $3 million to change that reality. What followed was one of conservation's quieter revolutions: by 2023, they had created or expanded 18 no-fishing zones across 310 miles of coastline, tripling the total protected seascapes in Turkish waters.

The breakthrough wasn't policy alone—it was trust. When skeptical local fishermen heard from their peers in Gökova, who had already witnessed larger catches after an earlier marine protected area was established there in 2012, resistance melted into participation. Kızılkaya trained locals as marine rangers to patrol the waters where coast guard staff had no capacity to enforce protections. Their work paid off strikingly: illegal fishing fell 80%. Within years, sandbar sharks returned to their only year-round Mediterranean home, and over 30 endangered monk seals now inhabit the region.

Yet Kızılkaya remains focused on the larger vision. Species migrate. Protected areas alone aren't enough if animals leave them and face renewed threats. The project now works to establish ecological corridors linking crucial habitats along the entire coastline—ensuring that the recovery doesn't stop at invisible borders. For a man recognized with the 2023 Goldman Environmental Prize, the real measure of success is the fishermen reporting better catches and an entire community rediscovering what thriving seas can provide.
